stories.title: The Girl Who Ate Six Seeds
stories.region: Eleusis and the grain plains of Attica

sources.ref: Homeric Hymn to Demeter (Hymn 2), lines 1–495
sources.note: Standard line numbering; the pomegranate seeds and the division of the year are at the close.

sources.ref: Foley, The Homeric Hymn to Demeter: Translation, Commentary, and Interpretive Essays (Princeton, 1994)
sources.note: Facing-page text with commentary; used to confirm the line numbering and the seed count.

sources.ref: Leeming, The Oxford Companion to World Mythology (2005)

stories.canonicalVersion: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter—Persephone eats the pomegranate seeds and must return below for part of every year.
stories.canonicalRationale: The oldest continuous telling that survives, and the only one that gives the bargain its exact terms. Later Roman versions (Ovid) change the seed count and add material; the Hymn is the textual floor.
variants: Ovid, Fasti IV and Metamorphoses V give the Roman telling and a different seed count
Apollodorus, Bibliotheca I.5 compresses the account
stories.variantNote: Greek tellers did not agree on how many seeds Persephone ate; the oldest written version says six.
stories.restrictionNote: Ancient Greek religious practice is not a living tradition and the Eleusinian material used here is the public narrative layer. The Mysteries themselves were secret in antiquity and their initiation content is not reconstructed or invented here—the story stops where the sources stop.
stories.ageAdaptationNote: The source opens with Hades seizing Persephone. This telling begins after the seizure—the reader learns she was taken and that her mother searched—because AGE_POLICY §2.8 requires narrating from the consequence, not the act. Nothing is softened: she is taken, Demeter’s grief is not resolved, and winter is the cost.

stories.title: The Weaver Who Would Not Look Down
stories.region: Hypaepa in Lydia, and Mount Tmolus

sources.ref: Ovid, Metamorphoses VI.1–145
sources.note: Standard book and line numbering; the weaving contest and the transformation.

sources.ref: Anderson, Ovid's Metamorphoses Books 6–10, edited with introduction and commentary (Oklahoma, 1972)
Leeming, The Oxford Companion to World Mythology (2005)

stories.canonicalVersion: Ovid’s Metamorphoses VI—Arachne out-weaves Athena, is struck, and is changed into a spider.
stories.canonicalRationale: Ovid is the only continuous narrative source; everything earlier is a passing mention. Choosing Ovid is choosing the only telling that actually tells the story, and the record says so plainly.
variants: Virgil, Georgics IV.246 mentions the spider without the contest
Pliny, Natural History VII.196 credits Arachne with inventing linen and nets
stories.variantNote: Only one ancient writer told this story from beginning to end, so this is his version.
stories.restrictionNote: No living tradition claims this narrative and no restricted material is involved. Screened for the separate risk that the tapestry Ovid describes depicts assaults by the gods: that catalogue is not reproduced (AGE_POLICY §2.8).
stories.ageAdaptationNote: In Ovid, Arachne’s tapestry is a catalogue of gods assaulting women, and Athena strikes her before the change. This telling says the tapestry showed the gods behaving badly and does not itemise it; the blow is one sentence, the change is the scene (AGE_POLICY §2.1, §2.8).

plot.door: A dyer's daughter is weaving in the doorway while a crowd watches her hands.
plot.pressure: An old woman warns her to show respect; Arachne answers that skill is skill.
plot.turn: The goddess drops her disguise, and Arachne's cloth turns out to be the better one.
plot.outcome: Arachne is changed, and keeps weaving — which is the part that stings.

stories.title: Wings Made in a Locked Room
stories.region: Crete and the sea east of it

sources.ref: Ovid, Metamorphoses VIII.183–235
sources.note: Standard book and line numbering; the making of the wings and the fall.

sources.ref: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca, Epitome I.12–13
sources.note: Independent ancient summary of the escape from Crete.

sources.ref: Gantz, Early Greek Myth: A Guide to Literary and Artistic Sources (Johns Hopkins, 1993)

stories.canonicalVersion: Ovid’s Metamorphoses VIII, checked against Apollodorus—Daedalus builds wings, Icarus flies too high, the wax fails.
stories.canonicalRationale: Ovid gives the fullest scene and Apollodorus confirms its outline independently, which satisfies the two-source rule with a genuinely separate ancient witness rather than a second summary of the same text.
variants: Some ancient writers say Icarus drowned after falling from a boat, not from the sky
Diodorus Siculus IV.77 rationalises the flight
stories.variantNote: Not every ancient writer believed in the wings; one says the boy simply fell from a boat.
stories.restrictionNote: Ancient Greek material with no living-tradition restriction. Screened also for the fact that Daedalus’s earlier work built the Labyrinth for the Minotaur; that thread is mentioned as background only and its violence is not staged.
stories.ageAdaptationNote: The source has Icarus drown and Daedalus find the feathers on the water. Nothing is softened—the boy dies and his father buries him. The drowning itself is one sentence and the body is not described (AGE_POLICY §2.2).

stories.title: The Bride Who Ate an Ox
stories.region: Ásgarðr and the land of the giants

sources.ref: Þrymskviða (Poetic Edda), stanzas 1–32
sources.note: Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to; standard stanza numbering.

sources.ref: Lindow, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford, 2001)
Larrington (trans.), The Poetic Edda (Oxford World's Classics, rev. ed. 2014)

stories.canonicalVersion: Þrymskviða in the Poetic Edda—Thor’s hammer is stolen and he recovers it disguised as a bride.
stories.canonicalRationale: Þrymskviða is a single complete poem with fixed stanza numbering and no competing version; there is nothing to choose between, and the record says so rather than implying a decision was made.
variants: Snorri does not retell this poem in the Prose Edda
Later Scandinavian ballads (Þrymlur, Torsvisen) retell it with changes
stories.variantNote: This poem survives in one Icelandic book, copied about seven hundred and fifty years ago.
stories.restrictionNote: Medieval Icelandic manuscript material. Modern Ásatrú and Forn Siðr communities exist and are referred to in the present tense where relevant, but the Edda poems are published texts and are not their closed material.
stories.ageAdaptationNote: The poem ends with Thor killing Thrym and the wedding guests. The consequence is told in two sentences and the killing is not staged (AGE_POLICY §2.1). The comedy of the disguise, which is the point of the poem, is kept whole.

stories.title: The Goddess Who Kept the Apples

sources.ref: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Skáldskaparmál 1–2 (the Þjazi episode)
sources.note: Standard chapter division of Skáldskaparmál.

sources.ref: Haustlǫng by Þjóðólfr of Hvinir, stanzas 1–13
sources.note: Ninth-century skaldic poem quoted by Snorri; independent and much older witness to the same episode.

sources.ref: Lindow, Norse Mythology (Oxford, 2001)

stories.canonicalVersion: Snorri’s Skáldskaparmál, cross-checked against the far older skaldic poem Haustlǫng, which describes the same abduction.
stories.canonicalRationale: Haustlǫng predates Snorri by roughly three centuries and is not derived from him, so the two together are a genuine independent pair rather than one text and its summary.
variants: Haustlǫng is fragmentary and describes the scene as a painting on a shield
Lokasenna 17 refers to Idun without the apple episode
stories.variantNote: Part of this story survives only as a poem describing pictures painted on a shield.
stories.restrictionNote: Medieval Icelandic material, published and unrestricted. No closed or ceremonial content is involved.
stories.ageAdaptationNote: Snorri has Þjazi burned to death when he flies into Ásgarðr. The outcome is stated; the burning is not described (AGE_POLICY §2.1). Idun’s abduction is told from the moment she is gone, not as a seizure scene.

stories.title: The Ribbon That Held a Wolf
stories.region: Ásgarðr and the island of Lyngvi

sources.ref: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 34
sources.note: Standard chapter numbering; the making of Gleipnir and Tyr's hand.

sources.ref: Völuspá (Poetic Edda), stanzas 44–45 and 53–55
sources.note: Independent poetic witness to Fenrir's binding and release.

sources.ref: Lindow, Norse Mythology (Oxford, 2001)

stories.canonicalVersion: Snorri’s Gylfaginning 34 for the binding scene, with Völuspá confirming the frame.
stories.canonicalRationale: Gylfaginning is the only text that narrates the trick in full; Völuspá independently confirms the wolf, the binding and the eventual release, so the choice rests on completeness plus corroboration rather than on preference.
variants: Völuspá gives no details of the ribbon or the hand
Lokasenna 38–39 refers to Tyr’s missing hand
stories.variantNote: The oldest poem about this wolf never explains how the gods tied him; that detail comes from a later Icelandic book.
stories.restrictionNote: Medieval Icelandic manuscript material, published and unrestricted.
stories.ageAdaptationNote: Tyr loses his hand. The source says the wolf bit it off; this telling says the same in one sentence and does not describe the wound (AGE_POLICY §2.1). Fenrir is frightening by scale and by what everyone knows is coming, not by anatomy (§2.4).

stories.region: Emain Macha and the plain of Muirthemne

sources.ref: Táin Bó Cúailnge, Recension I (Book of the Dun Cow / Yellow Book of Lecan), the Macgnímrada or Boyhood Deeds section
sources.note: The boyhood-deeds episodes are a discrete titled section of the Táin.

sources.note: Standard critical edition with facing translation.

sources.ref: Koch (ed.), Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia (2006)

stories.canonicalVersion: The Boyhood Deeds section of Táin Bó Cúailnge, Recension I—Sétanta kills the smith’s hound and offers to serve in its place until a replacement is reared.
stories.canonicalRationale: Recension I is the earliest recoverable text of the Táin and O’Rahilly’s edition is the standard critical text; later recensions expand the episode with material the earliest witness does not have.
variants: Recension II (Book of Leinster) tells the episode at greater length
The Middle Irish Aided Chon Culainn gives his death, not his naming
stories.variantNote: Irish scribes copied this story for centuries, and each copy is a little longer than the last.
stories.restrictionNote: Medieval Irish manuscript material, published and digitised (CELT, University College Cork). No living restricted tradition governs it.
stories.ageAdaptationNote: A boy kills a guard dog with a ball and a stick. The source is direct about it; this telling states what he did and what it cost, and does not describe the animal’s injuries (AGE_POLICY §2.1, which flags violence toward an animal for special care).

stories.title: Nine Hundred Years on the Water
stories.region: Lough Derravaragh, the Sea of Moyle, and Erris

sources.ref: Oidheadh Chloinne Lir (The Tragic Death of the Children of Lir), Early Modern Irish text
sources.note: One of the Trí Truagha na Scéalaigheachta, the Three Sorrows of Storytelling.

sources.ref: O'Curry (ed. and trans.), "The Fate of the Children of Lir", Atlantis 4 (1863), 113–157
sources.note: First full scholarly edition with facing translation.

sources.ref: Koch (ed.), Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia (2006)

stories.canonicalVersion: Oidheadh Chloinne Lir in O’Curry’s edition—four children are turned into swans by their stepmother and spend nine hundred years on three waters.
stories.canonicalRationale: This is a single literary text with no competing narrative version; the choice is between editions, and O’Curry’s is the first complete scholarly one. The record names the edition rather than pretending the text is anonymous tradition.
variants: The tale’s Christian ending, in which the swans are baptised, is present in all manuscripts and is not a later addition
Modern retellings frequently drop the ending
stories.variantNote: The oldest written version ends with a bell and a priest; many modern books leave that out.
stories.restrictionNote: Medieval and early modern Irish literary material, published. No restricted content. Screened for the stepmother motif, which AGE_POLICY §2.9 flags for special review.
stories.ageAdaptationNote: Aoife is their stepmother and she does this out of jealousy. AGE_POLICY §2.9 requires that step-parent cruelty be measured and the outcome just: her act is one paragraph, her punishment is stated and not staged, and the children’s endurance—not her cruelty—is the story.

stories.title: The Machine Nobody Can Describe

stories.canonicalRationale: This papyrus is the only Egyptian text that narrates the dispute from beginning to end. Plutarch’s Greek account is far later, second-hand and foreign; using the Egyptian text is what keeps an Egyptian story in Egyptian hands.

stories.variantNote: The version most people know came from a Greek writer a thousand years later; this one is Egyptian.
stories.restrictionNote: Ancient Egyptian material, published and unrestricted; no living tradition governs it. A separate honesty duty applies: Egyptian writing did not record vowels, so the pronunciation guide states that its readings are a modern Egyptological convention rather than a recovered sound.
stories.ageAdaptationNote: The papyrus contains explicit sexual episodes between Seth and Horus and an act of mutilation. AGE_POLICY §2.8 places sexuality at OMIT with no exception: those episodes are absent, and the narrative is carried by the tribunal, the boat race and Isis’s disguises, which the source supports fully. The eye injury is stated in one sentence and its healing is the scene (§2.1).

stories.canonicalRationale: The Turin papyrus is the only substantial witness. It survives because it was written as a healing spell, which is itself worth telling the reader: the story was preserved because it was useful, not because it was literature.

stories.restrictionNote: Ancient Egyptian material, published and unrestricted. Screened for a specific temptation: because the surviving texts never reveal the hidden name, inventing one would be exactly the gap-filling SOURCING_STANDARD §10 forbids. The gap is kept and shown to the reader.
stories.ageAdaptationNote: Ra is bitten and suffers. AGE_POLICY §2.1 keeps the fact and drops the anatomy: he is in pain, the gods cannot help, and the pain is told in a sentence rather than staged across a page.

stories.canonicalRationale: There is exactly one manuscript, so there is no variant to choose between; the record states that plainly. Two independent scholarly editions confirm the reading.
variants: No other manuscript of this tale is known

stories.variantNote: Only one copy of this story has ever been found, and it is nearly four thousand years old.
stories.restrictionNote: Ancient Egyptian literary material, published and unrestricted. No living tradition or restricted content.
stories.ageAdaptationNote: The serpent’s family was destroyed by a falling star and he alone survived. The source states it and does not dwell; this telling does the same. The loss is not resolved or consoled away (AGE_POLICY §2.3), because the serpent’s point is that he is still here.

stories.title: The Chain Let Down from the Sky

stories.canonicalVersion: The Ilé-Ifẹ̀ creation narrative as recorded by Bascom from Yoruba narrators—Ọbàtálá is sent down with earth in a snail shell, and does not finish the job.
stories.canonicalRationale: Bascom recorded from named practitioners in Yoruba with facing translation, and Idowu writes as a Yoruba scholar of his own tradition. Pairing an outside ethnographer with an inside scholar is deliberate: neither is left to speak alone.
variants: Some narrators give the task to Odùduwà rather than Ọbàtálá
Ifẹ̀ and Ọ̀yọ́ traditions differ on the order of events
stories.variantNote: Yoruba narrators do not agree on who came down the chain first, and the disagreement is old and serious.
stories.restrictionNote: Bascom’s texts were recorded and published with the participation of named diviners; the narrative layer is public. Used as narrative only, never as divination instruction: which odù governs what, ẹbọ prescriptions and initiation content are excluded. Òrìṣà worship continues today in Nigeria, Brazil and Cuba, so the present tense is used.
stories.ageAdaptationNote: In several tellings Ọbàtálá drinks palm wine, falls asleep and leaves the work unfinished, which is also given as the origin of people born with disabilities. That aetiology is not reproduced: it would frame disabled readers as a mistake. The unfinished work is kept; the explanation attached to it is dropped, and this is recorded here because a reader may meet it elsewhere (AGE_POLICY §2.15, §2.16).

variants: Tellings differ on how many òrìṣà were sent and on what finally persuades her
Òṣogbo traditions emphasise the river covenant
stories.variantNote: The number of gods sent down changes from teller to teller; the point of the story does not.
stories.restrictionNote: Public narrative layer of a living tradition, recorded and published with named narrators. Divination procedure, ẹbọ prescriptions and initiation content are excluded. variants: Narrators differ on why the chameleon delayed—eating berries, or simply being slow

stories.restrictionNote: Public narrative genre (izinganekwane and origin traditions), recorded with named narrators and published in Zulu. Not restricted. Excluded: isangoma initiation knowledge, muthi preparation, and family-specific amadlozi practice.

stories.canonicalRationale: Two independent field records, separated by forty years and by region, with named narrators in Rasmussen’s case. Neither is a retelling of the other, which is exactly what the two-source rule is for.

stories.restrictionNote: Published field ethnography from named narrators; the narrative layer is not restricted. plot.turn: She goes under, and what happens to her hands becomes every animal in the sea.

stories.canonicalRationale: Two independent field records again. This narrative is chosen alongside Sedna because the two together show the range of the tradition: one is cosmological, one is domestic and sharp.

stories.canonicalRationale: One manuscript survives, so the choice is between translations, and two independent scholarly translations are cited rather than one. Christenson supplies the line numbering used here.
variants: Christenson and Tedlock differ on the reading of several passages

stories.variantNote: Painted pots made a thousand years before the book was written show scenes from this story that the book does not include.
stories.restrictionNote: Published sixteenth-century K’iche' text with a surviving manuscript and multiple critical translations; not restricted. Maya peoples are living peoples and K’iche' is a living language, so present tense is used for them. stories.ageAdaptationNote: The twins are killed more than once and the lords of Xibalba set lethal traps. AGE_POLICY §2.2 allows death plainly and §2.1 keeps the killings to their outcome. variants: Christenson and Tedlock differ on the description of the wooden people

stories.restrictionNote: Published K’iche' text with surviving manuscript; not restricted. Present tense for living Maya peoples and for the K’iche' language. Same exclusions as the companion record.
stories.ageAdaptationNote: The wooden people are destroyed and the source describes their own tools and animals turning on them. The destruction is told; the assault is not staged (AGE_POLICY §2.1, §2.17). The failure of the earlier attempts is kept, because a creation story in which the makers do not fail is a different story.

plot.pressure: Mud will not hold its shape, and wood holds its shape but cannot remember anything.
plot.turn: The wooden people are wiped out, and the makers try a third time with ground maize.

stories.title: The Small God Who Jumped First

sources.ref: Sahagún, Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España (Florentine Codex), Book VII, chapter 2
sources.note: Nahuatl text with Spanish, compiled from Nahua elders and written by Nahua scribes; Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana.

sources.ref: Anderson & Dibble (trans.), Florentine Codex: General History of the Things of New Spain, Book 7 — The Sun, Moon, and Stars (School of American Research / University of Utah, 1953–1982)
sources.note: Standard translation from the Nahuatl.

sources.note: Independent Nahuatl manuscript giving the same succession of suns.

stories.canonicalVersion: Florentine Codex Book VII—the gods gather in the dark at Teotihuacan and the small scabbed god goes into the fire before the rich one.
stories.canonicalRationale: The Florentine Codex was compiled from Nahua elders and written down by Nahua scribes in Nahuatl, and the Leyenda de los Soles confirms the account independently. Both are Nahuatl-language witnesses rather than Spanish summaries.
variants: The Leyenda de los Soles orders the five suns slightly differently
The Historia de los Mexicanos por sus pinturas gives another arrangement
stories.variantNote: Nahua sources do not fully agree on the order of the earlier suns, and this book follows the fullest one.
stories.restrictionNote: Published sixteenth-century Nahuatl material with surviving manuscripts; not restricted. Nahua peoples are living peoples and Nahuatl is spoken today. Two framing rules apply: sacrifice is presented as a cost the community accepted, never as spectacle, and the phrase 'they were like that' is forbidden.
stories.ageAdaptationNote: The gods throw themselves into a fire so the sun will move, and afterwards more blood is required. AGE_POLICY §2.7 places sacrifice at IMPLY with review: the fact and its meaning are given, the fire is one sentence, and no ceremony is described. The framing rule in §2.7 is decisive here—this is told as something that cost the gods everything, which is what the source says.
